sounds.intro: Nobody recorded Plato's voice, but the Attic of his day can be reconstructed closely. The evidence includes spellings and misspellings on Athenian inscriptions, the descriptions of ancient grammarians, how Greek words were written in Latin and other languages, the rhythms of verse, and even animal noises: the comic poet Cratinus has a sheep bleat βῆ βῆ. This guide follows W. Sidney Allen's Vox Graeca, the standard account. The vowels and consonants are well established; the exact melody of the accent is less certain.

tips.p: The accent marks record melody, not stress: on the accented syllable the voice rose in pitch. Dionysius of Halicarnassus, writing in Rome in the late 1st century BC, says speech rose and fell within about a musical fifth (On Literary Composition 11). Rhythm came from vowel length instead, which is why Greek verse is built from long and short syllables.

The acute ά marks a rise. The circumflex ᾶ, found only on long vowels and diphthongs, is a rise and fall within one syllable. The grave ὰ replaces an acute on a final syllable when another word follows, and probably means the rise was cancelled or reduced.

Always on one of the last three syllables, and no further back than the second-to-last if the last syllable is long. Most modern readers say the accented syllable louder, as a stress. That is a practical compromise, not the ancient sound.
η and ω are always long, ε and ο always short, while α, ι and υ can be either. Holding long vowels about twice as long as short ones lets you hear the rhythm of the poetry.

In 1528 Erasmus argued that Greek should be read as it once sounded. His 'Erasmian' system is still what most schools teach, usually with a stress accent and local habits: English speakers often say θ as in 'thin', φ as f and χ as in 'loch'. Greece reads ancient texts in modern pronunciation, where η, ι, υ, ει and οι all sound like 'ee', αι is 'e', β is v, δ is the 'th' of 'this', there is no h, no vowel length and the accent is a stress. Both work for reading, but neither is how Plato sounded.
The vowels and consonants rest on solid evidence. Less certain are the exact melody of the accent, the dates of changes such as ου becoming [uː], and whether ζ was zd or dz.

grammar.title: To be: εἰμί
grammar.note: Every form except εἶ is enclitic: it leans on the word before and often loses its accent. The plurals arrive in unit 8.

grammar.title: The article: ὁ, ἡ, τό
grammar.note: Greek's word for 'the' shows gender, number and case. Unit 3 teaches the subject and object, unit 8 the genitive and plural subject, unit 11 the dative and plural object.

grammar.title: Second declension: ὁ ἵππος, τὸ βιβλίον
grammar.note: Mostly masculine nouns in -ος and neuters in -ον. Neuters look the same as subject and object, and their plural ends in -α.

grammar.title: First declension: ἀδελφή, οἰκία, θάλαττα
grammar.note: Mostly feminine nouns in -η or -α. After ε, ι or ρ the α stays through the singular. Nouns in short -α, like θάλαττα, switch to η in the genitive and dative. All share one set of plural endings.

grammar.title: Adjectives: καλός, καλή, καλόν
grammar.note: An adjective takes the gender, number and case of its noun. After ε, ι or ρ the feminine has α: μικρός, μικρά, μικρόν.

grammar.title: Present tense: λέγω 'I say'
grammar.note: The ending shows the person, so no pronoun is needed. γράφω, ἔχω, βλέπω and most verbs in -ω work the same way.

grammar.title: The aorist: ἔγραψα, ἔφυγον, εἶπον
grammar.note: The augment ἐ- marks the past. First aorists add σ and -α endings; second aorists change the stem and take -ον endings. εἶπον serves as the past of λέγω.

grammar.title: Third declension: παῖς, σῶμα, πόλις, βασιλεύς
grammar.note: The nominative often hides the stem, and the genitive shows it. In Plato's day the plural of βασιλεύς was βασιλῆς; βασιλεῖς replaced it after about 350 BC.

grammar.title: Middle voice: γίγνομαι 'I become'
grammar.note: Middle-only verbs such as βούλομαι, ἔρχομαι and μάχομαι use these endings. Attic prose spells 'you' with -ει; some editions print -ῃ.

grammar.title: Infinitives
grammar.note: Active infinitives end in -ειν or -αι, middle ones in -σθαι. The present describes an ongoing action, the aorist a single one; the course uses the present.

grammar.note: Participles decline like adjectives. The masculine and neuter of λέγων and ὤν follow the third declension (stem λεγοντ-, ὀντ-), the feminine the first.

grammar.title: Numbers 1 to 10
grammar.note: One to four change with gender and case; five upwards never change. Greeks also wrote numbers with letters marked by a stroke. Early Attic prose and most other Greeks said τέσσαρες for four.

grammar.title: The future: γράψω, ὄψομαι
grammar.note: The future adds σ to the stem and uses the present endings. Several common verbs have middle futures, such as ὄψομαι 'I will see' and ἀκούσομαι 'I will hear'.

grammar.title: To be: present, past and future
grammar.note: The past is an imperfect, 'was, used to be'. The future is middle in form; ἔσται has no vowel before its ending.
